name: Launch drones
summary: The unit sends out small drones or minions, on a key or as add-ons bought for it, that fly or run around it and act on their own for a while: they attack what their owner attacks, scout ahead, or mend and shield allies, then come back, run out or are shot down. Each drone has its own small health, so the enemy can shoot the drones down, splash a bunched swarm, switch them off with EMP, slip out of their leash or kill the owner, whose death usually takes them too. In the piloted variant the owner stands still while the player steers one drone by hand within a short leash. The pattern is the release on a key; drones that are simply a unit's always-on gun are the weapon family drone-launcher instead.
counterplay: Shoot the drones down: they are small and fragile, so anti-air guns, flak and steady rifle fire pick them off, and the owner loses most of his damage with them (Tempest Rising's Drone Operator, whose drone is a small aircraft that anti-air weapons can shoot down).
Splash the swarm: drones and minions bunch up, so area damage clears a whole wave at once (Psionic Storm and Archons against StarCraft II Locusts).
Switch them off: EMP destroys the Generals Battle Drone, and hacking stops Overwatch's summoned B.O.B. for a few seconds.

Kill or catch the owner: most drones die or drop when their owner dies (Generals vehicle drones, Tempest Rising's Combat Drone), and a player piloting a drone stands still and exposed (Apex Legends' Crypto, Tempest Rising's Drone Operator).

Weather the wave, then push: released drones expire after a set time and the key then cools down for a long while, so defenders who survive a Locust wave strike back before the next one comes (StarCraft II Swarm Host).

Pull them off target: drones are leashed, so breaking line of sight or leaving their reach sends them back (Valorant's Wingman returns to a straight run once his target slips beyond his detection reach; Crypto's drone is pulled home when it strays too far), and cheap bait can draw a wave away from its real target (Terran players tease Carrier interceptors with flying buildings).

Deny the pick-up: when a spent minion must be collected before the ability comes back (Gekko's globules in Valorant), holding the spot where it fell keeps its owner from reclaiming it before it fades (reasoned from the reclaim rule).

other_examples.note: The Swarm Host never attacks by itself: a manually triggered ability hatches a pair of Locusts that do its fighting, cross terrain in flight and drop down with Swoop to attack, and die after a short timed life while the ability waits through a long cooldown. The player steers where each wave goes, the waves cost nothing, and players pair hosts with Nydus Worms to pop out, spawn and escape. Defenders answer with splash (Psionic Storm, Archons), static defences and stasis traps, by counter-attacking while the hosts cool down, and by hunting the hosts, which are helpless without their Locusts.

sources.title: Swarm Host, Liquipedia StarCraft II Wiki

other_examples.unit: Battle Drone, Scout Drone and Hellfire Drone (USA vehicle add-ons)
other_examples.note: USA vehicles buy one drone each as an upgrade, and a lost drone can be bought again. The Battle Drone trails its vehicle, machine-guns infantry and patches up its parent while the parent stands still; the Scout Drone circles nearby, widens the vehicle's sight so it can use its full weapon reach, and reveals stealthed units; the Zero Hour Hellfire Drone fires missiles in its parent's defence, which makes it an escort for unarmed support vehicles. Each drone falls when its parent dies, and EMP destroys the Battle Drone.

other_examples.unit: Carrier (Protoss): Release Interceptors and Interceptor rebuilds
other_examples.note: The Carrier's normal attack, Interceptors it sends at targets in range that fly home when the target dies or the Carrier pulls back past a leash, is a weapon (the drone-launcher family here). Two parts fit this pattern: lost Interceptors are trained again for a few minerals each, an order that can run on autocast, and for part of Legacy of the Void a Release Interceptors ability flung every Interceptor out at long range, where the survivors died after a set time; patch 3.8.0 removed it. Interceptors no longer heal between sorties, so anti-air positions grind them down, and splash such as the Archon's kills them in numbers.

An upgrade on the back of the UEF commander (and of support commanders) adds a small drone that helps with whatever its owner is building, or can be sent off on its own to build, repair, reclaim or capture somewhere else at the same rate: a worker drone rather than a fighter.

shooter_analogues.note: Gekko sends Wingman running ahead: the creature bounces off walls, watches a wide cone in front of it, chases an enemy it spots with an audible cue and claps out a concussing blast; with the alternate fire it carries the Spike to plant it or runs to defuse it instead. It can be shot, and when it is done, out of time or killed it becomes a dormant globule that Gekko has to walk over and reclaim before it vanishes, after which the ability comes back on a cooldown. Skye's ultimate sends up to three Seekers, one per enemy, each heading for the nearest enemy left on the map; they can be shot, the target is warned as one closes in, and a Seeker that arrives leaves its target nearsighted and slowed.

Ashe's ultimate drops her robot sidekick just ahead of her; it rushes in the direction she aims, tossing up any enemies it rams, then stops at an enemy, a wall or the end of its run and shoots nearby enemies like a turret for a while, preferring targets Ashe has hit. It counts as an extra player for contesting objectives and can be healed, boosted or hacked, which shuts it down briefly.

shooter_analogues.unit: Drone skill (Striker, Defender, Bombardier, Fixer and Tactician)
shooter_analogues.note: An agent's skill slot holds one drone that hovers above them, in one of five builds: a Striker that shoots nearby enemies or the ones it is ordered onto, a Defender that knocks incoming bullets aside for its owner or a chosen ally (each deflection shortens its life, and it can't guard itself), a Bombardier that makes a bombing run along a strip the player marks, a Fixer that mends armour on its owner or on a picked teammate, and a Tactician that climbs above a chosen spot and marks hostiles for the group. After each use the skill cools down for longer or shorter depending on whether the player dismissed the drone, enemies shot it down or its time ran out.

Called down by stratagem and worn as a backpack, the drone lifts off to hover around its wearer and shoots nearby enemies by itself, sticking to its first target until it loses sight of it, even while the wearer sprints. It flies back to the pack to reload from a limited reserve that resupplies refill, and the backpack key calls it home and keeps it docked until pressed again.

shooter_analogues.unit: MAV and EOD Bot (Battlefield 3 and 4 gadgets)
shooter_analogues.note: Two gadgets the soldier steers by remote. The Recon's MAV is an unarmed flying camera: it spots enemies, its motion sensor pings moving enemies on the team's minimap, and it can jam and destroy enemy gadgets; in Battlefield 3, ramming an enemy to death destroys the MAV too. The Engineer's EOD Bot is a small tracked robot that repairs friendly vehicles, disposes of explosives and arms or disarms Rush objectives; one rocket destroys it, and a new one comes from an ammo box.

Crypto throws out a drone and can take control of it, flying it up to a set distance from himself; past a further limit it is pulled back on its own, and when he stops piloting it stays parked in the air. While he flies it he stands still and is wide open. Recalling it takes a moment and restores its health; it can open doors and bins and collect fallen squadmates' banners, his passive reveals enemies near it to his squad, and his ultimate fires an EMP from it.

A drone that keeps a lone miner company only in solo play and destroys itself when a second player joins. It shoots threats within reach of both itself and the player, attacks, mines or lights whatever the player marks with a laser pointer, fires rockets at a marked target from a few charges that recover over time, and revives the downed player from a limited number of charges. The shout key makes it drop its task and fly back. Enemies ignore it and it can't be destroyed; its upgrades are bought at a terminal on the space rig.

Gaige's action skill calls up a floating robot that fights for her with claw swipes, and with an electric bolt against fliers and targets out of reach, passing through walls to get at enemies. It stays for a fixed time, and the cooldown only starts once it leaves; skills in her trees add attacks, let it copy her shield, or have it restore allies' shields.

player_translation.summary: A drone-carrying unit (an operator soldier, a carrier vehicle, a flying fortress) presses one key to release a few small drones or minions. They follow it on a short leash and attack what it shoots, scout ahead, or mend and shield teammates, for a limited time or until shot down; then they come home or expire, and the key cools down. Drones let one player pressure around corners and beyond their own reach, but they are fragile, leashed and loud, so the enemy gets clear answers: shoot them, splash them, EMP them, or catch the owner. The piloted variant swaps the player's body for one drone for a while.
as_user: Press Q to release your drones: two to four small fliers (more at the top tier) that spread around you, stay inside a short leash, and attack whatever you hit last, or the nearest enemy in sight if you hit nothing.

Hold Q, aim and release to send them to the spot under your cursor: they fly there, attack what they find, and come back when the target dies or you move past the leash, the way StarCraft II players steer a Locust wave.

They last a set time or until shot down. The cooldown starts once the last one is back or gone; calling them home early while they still live shortens it, and losing them all lengthens it (The Division 2 times its drone cooldown by how the drone ended).
Your HUD shows how many drones are out, their health and the time left; their kills and assists count as yours.

In the piloted variant you tap Q to launch one drone and hold Q to take it over: your body stands still and exposed while you fly inside the leash, and taking damage throws you back into it, much as Tempest Rising's Drone Operator and Apex Legends' Crypto stand still while they fly.
In the bought add-on variant there is no key: you buy one drone of a type at a depot or on the spawn screen, it follows you until it is shot down, and you buy it again (Generals' vehicle drones).
as_target: Drones are small, team-coloured fliers or runners with a buzz of their own; when one picks you, you hear a chirp and see a direction marker, as a Valorant Seeker's target is warned when it closes in.
Right now you can shoot them (they have little health), throw splash into the bunch, use an EMP to drop them all, break line of sight, or run past their owner's leash so they turn back.
Or go for the owner: drones drop or go dormant when the owner dies, and a piloting owner stands still somewhere close by.
Once a wave is spent its owner waits out a long cooldown; that is the moment to push.
teammates: The owner's team uses drones to scout and screen: they spot over walls, soak a few shots and pin a target that a teammate then finishes, as Gekko's Wingman concusses a defender for his team.
Support builds send a drone to a teammate to repair, heal or turn bullets aside for them (The Division 2's Fixer and Defender), which makes the owner a protector.
Anti-air and EMP players become counter-picks: one flak gunner can strip a drone carrier of most of its damage, as anti-air does to Tempest Rising's Drone Operator.
A piloting operator needs a bodyguard: a teammate guards the planted body while they fly.

Several drone units on one team stack into a swarm that overwhelms single targets; Tempest Rising's makers called Skycranes packed with Drone Operators a tactic that worked too well, which is why caps per player and per team matter.
controls: Move with WASD and aim with the mouse; left mouse fires your own weapon, and your drones attack what you hit.
Q: tap to release the drones around you; hold, aim and release to send them to the cursor; tap again while they are out to call them home, refunding part of the cooldown.

Piloted variant: tap Q to launch the drone, hold Q to take control; WASD and the mouse steer it, left mouse fires its gun or tool, and Q returns you to your body. The camera slides to the drone and the leash ring stays on screen.
Bought add-on variant: no key; the drone acts on its own and is bought again at a depot or on respawn.
Reclaim variant: walk over your dormant drone, or press the interact key beside it, to pick it up.
The pattern spends one counted key (Q).
feedback: Release: a hatch sound and the drones fanning out from the unit, each with a team-coloured light and a shadow on the ground so it reads over terrain from above.
Lock-on: a thin line from a drone to its target and a chirp the target hears, with a direction marker on the target's screen.
Leash: a faint ring around the owner while drones are out; drones flying home draw a short trail.
Owner's HUD: drone icons with health, a timer bar, and a sound when one is shot down.
Piloting: the owner's planted body shows a link halo to everyone, so enemies can find the operator.
Dormant drone: a glowing pick-up with a shrinking ring for the time left, visible to both teams.
changes_from_rts: In StarCraft II the Carrier's interceptors are its gun and fight all the time; here the release is a key with a cooldown, so drones come in visible waves the enemy can wait out. A unit whose drones are always out takes the drone-launcher weapon family instead, as the Drone Operator's Combat Drone does.

RTS drones are bought per unit and rebuilt for money or for free over time (Generals add-ons, Carrier rebuilds, Tempest Rising's Drone Factory). Here a lost drone costs time, a longer cooldown, or in the add-on variant a rebuy at the depot.
The RTS player micromanages a swarm; one player has one body, so drones get simple rules: follow, attack the owner's last target, come back at the leash.

A Carrier fields eight interceptors and the Vimana six Servitors and a Caretaker. With up to 48 players each unit puts out only a few drones, capped per team, so the screen stays readable and the server keeps up.

Early in StarCraft II's Legacy of the Void, the computer opponent shot interceptors before the Carriers themselves, and only patch 5.0.11 in January 2023 made attackers prefer other targets (Liquipedia); drones that draw fire like that shield their owner for free. Human players choose their targets, so drones should die fast and their loss should cost the owner cooldown.
The Tempest Rising operator's root and leash carry straight over; a top-down camera makes piloting easy, because the view only has to slide to the drone inside the leash.
The Vimana's summon also calls a whole lasting unit (a Caretaker); on a player's unit the summon stays small minions that expire, and summoning a lasting unit would be a different pattern.

team_play.notes: Drones give the owner's team eyes and a screen (scouting over walls, soaking shots, pinning a target for a teammate's finish), support builds make the owner a protector, and a piloting operator needs a bodyguard. On the other side they create counter-picks: one anti-air or EMP player strips a drone unit of most of its damage. Several drone units on one team stack into a swarm, which Tempest Rising's makers saw when Skycranes packed with Drone Operators worked too well.

notes: Each drone is a small AI agent that must follow, pick targets, get around or over obstacles and return, simulated on the server for dozens of players at once; flying drones need simple steering rather than full pathfinding.
Network cost: with 48 players and a few drones each, snapshots carry hundreds of small moving entities, so drones need compact state and caps per player and per team.
Rules: leash distance, lifetime, recall with a partial refund, death with the owner, kill credit to the owner, and cleanup when the owner switches unit or leaves.
Interactions: anti-air targeting must see drones; splash, EMP and hacking must affect them; players must be able to shoot them without drones confusing target selection against real players.
The piloted variant needs a control handoff: the camera slides to the drone, inputs go to it, the body stays behind as a vulnerable object, and damage hands control back.
UI: drone icons and timers, lock-on lines and warnings, the leash ring, and a pick-up marker for the reclaim variant.
Drone spam: many drones from many players clutter the screen and load the server; cap drones per player and per team.
Drones that never miss or chase anywhere (Valorant's Seekers lock onto enemies anywhere on the map) take play away from their target; give them lock-on warnings, a slow approach and low health.
Free soak: if drones cost nothing to lose and enemies shoot them first, they shield the owner for free; losing them must lengthen the cooldown.
Riskless scouting over walls breaks hiding; leash the drone, root the owner and show where the owner stands while piloting.
Hard-counter swings: a drone unit is strong when the enemy brings no anti-air or EMP and weak when it does; keep the owner's own weapon useful, as Tempest Rising's operator keeps an anti-tank pistol.
Drones are small; from a top-down camera they need bold silhouettes, team colours, ground shadows and a sound so players can see and hear them.
Players must tell drones from projectiles and from real units, and a fighting drone from a support one; a distinct shape per job does it.
Who owns a drone, and whether its owner is piloting, must be clear: a link line or halo between owner and drones.

variants.name: Timed wave
variants.summary: A key releases a wave of short-lived drones or minions that run or fly at a chosen spot or at the nearest enemies and expire after a few seconds. A long cooldown spaces the waves out, so the enemy can weather one and strike back; some waves are free (Swarm Host Locusts), while others charge a price on every use (the Vimana's summon).
variants.seen_in: StarCraft II Swarm Host Locusts, Valorant Skye's Seekers, Tempest Rising Vimana's Combat Servitors, StarCraft II Carrier's removed Release Interceptors

variants.name: Bought add-on drone
variants.summary: No key: the unit buys one drone of a type (a gun drone, a scout drone, a repair drone) that follows it for good until shot down and is bought again; it falls when its owner dies.
variants.seen_in: Generals USA Battle, Scout and Hellfire Drones; Deep Rock Galactic Bosco (a companion only in solo play)

variants.name: Scout drone
variants.summary: The drone does not fight: it widens its owner's sight, reveals stealthed units near him, or climbs above a chosen spot and marks enemies there for the team.
variants.seen_in: Generals Scout Drone, The Division 2 Tactician Drone, Battlefield MAV, Apex Legends Crypto's drone

adds_strengths.why: Its drone sees over walls and around corners and marks enemies for the team, so its side fights with better information.

counters.why: The scout drone reveals stealthed units around its owner (Generals Scout Drone), so infiltrators lose their cover.

variants.name: Piloted drone
variants.summary: The owner plants himself and steers one drone by hand inside a leash, to scout over cliffs and walls, mark targets or strike from beyond the enemy's reach; his body stands still and exposed, and losing the drone or taking damage hands control back.
variants.seen_in: Tempest Rising Drone Operator (Remote Control Drone), Apex Legends Crypto's Surveillance Drone, Battlefield MAV and EOD Bot

adds_weaknesses.why: While flying the drone the owner can't move and is easy to kill, and the drone can't leave a short leash around him.

variants.name: Support drone
variants.summary: The drone mends armour or hulls, heals, turns bullets aside or helps build instead of fighting, and can be sent to a teammate; it can't defend itself.
variants.seen_in: The Division 2 Fixer and Defender Drones, Supreme Commander Engineering Drone, Generals Battle Drone (patches up its parent while it stands still), Deep Rock Galactic Bosco (revives)

adds_strengths.why: Keeps repairing, healing or shielding a chosen teammate while its owner fights, so a push outlasts chip damage.

adds_weaknesses.why: The drone can't defend itself, and the teammate it guards becomes the obvious target.

variants.name: Recall and reclaim
variants.summary: Drones fly home to rearm or when called, and the ability returns sooner; or a spent minion falls dormant where it finished, and its owner must walk over and pick it up before it fades, or the ability stays lost for the full wait.
variants.seen_in: Valorant Gekko's globules, Helldivers 2 Guard Dog (docks to reload, recall key), The Division 2 drone cooldown by how it ended, Deep Rock Galactic Bosco (shout recall), Apex Legends Crypto (recall restores the drone)

variants.name: Summoned brute
variants.summary: An ultimate summons one big minion that charges in the aimed direction, knocking enemies down, then stands and fights like a turret for a while; it counts as a player for objectives and can be healed, boosted or hacked.
variants.seen_in: Overwatch Ashe's B.O.B., Borderlands 2 Gaige's Deathtrap

variants.name: Objective runner
variants.summary: The minion is sent to do objective work for its owner: it carries a charge to plant, runs to defuse, or arms and disarms a target while the owner stays in cover, and drops what it carries if it is shot on the way.
variants.seen_in: Valorant Gekko's Wingman (plants and defuses the Spike), Battlefield EOD Bot (arms and disarms Rush objectives)

adds_strengths.why: Its drones strike around corners and beyond its owner's own reach and soak a few shots, so one player pressures two places at once.

adds_weaknesses.why: The drones are fragile and leashed, most fall when their owner dies, and once a wave is spent the owner waits out a long cooldown.

counters.why: Free, repeated drone waves wear down buildings and fixed defences from beyond their reach (StarCraft II Swarm Host waves; Tempest Rising's operator hitting defences from outside their range).
A turret wastes its fire on drones or is struck from outside its reach, as the Tempest Rising operator flies his drone at anti-infantry defences.

countered_by.why: Most drones fly, so anti-air guns and flak shoot them down and strip their owner of most of his damage (Tempest Rising's Drone Operator).
Drones and minions bunch up, so area damage clears a whole wave at once (Psionic Storm and Archons against StarCraft II Locusts).
EMP destroys drones outright (the Generals Battle Drone), and hacking shuts a summoned robot off for a moment (Overwatch's B.O.B.).
A fast flanker reaches the owner, whose drones fall when he dies, and a piloting operator stands still and can't fight back.

open_questions: How many drones per player, and what team-wide cap? This draft proposes two to four per player, more at the top tier.
Do drones die with their owner (Generals, Tempest Rising) or keep going until their time runs out?

Should the piloted variant stay inside launch-drones? The registry notes send a remote-piloted drone to the crew model remote, but that model is for a unit that is itself the remote body; the Drone Operator is coded as a solo soldier whose drone is his weapon, and his record relies on this variant. The other choice is a pattern of its own for steering a released drone by hand.
The Vimana's summon also brings a Caretaker, a full lasting unit; its fit note asks for a pattern for making units in the field. This draft covers only the short-lived Combat Servitors.
May drones capture or contest objectives (Overwatch's B.O.B. counts as a player; Valorant's Wingman plants and defuses), or only fight?
Do ground-running minions (Locusts once landed, Wingman, Seekers) count as ground targets for every weapon, while fliers need anti-air?

shooter_fit.reason: Drones and summoned minions are common in hero and squad shooters (Valorant, Overwatch, Apex Legends, The Division 2, Helldivers 2) and read well as a burst on a key, but small fliers are hard to see from a top-down camera and many drones from 48 players strain screen and server, so they need caps, bold silhouettes and clear warnings.
